packets.title: I Rebuilt the Chess Lesson Around the Decision

scenes.label: The move and the reason
scenes.narration: Two players can make the same move. One saw the threat. The other guessed. A board that only celebrates the move treats those two moments as equal. That bothered me while I was building Dark Castle Chess. I wanted the lesson to live in the choice, and to survive what happens next. In a moment, I will show you three real product screens: the position in Explore, the handoff into computer play, and the response with coaching. Watch one question travel through all three: what did the player notice before moving? I am not asking a game to read anyone's mind. I am asking the product to keep the position and its consequence visible long enough for a person to learn from them. Start with this board. Pause before the move. What would you protect, and what would you risk?

scenes.label: The position
scenes.narration: Explore is where the player can inspect a position before adding the pressure of a computer reply. The public gameplay capture shows the board in that learning state. This is where I want a player to slow down. A piece can be moved for many reasons: a threat, an opening, an escape, or a hope that the opponent does not see something. The screen can show the available position. It cannot prove why a person chose a square. So the lesson begins with a prompt to look, choose, and explain. I would ask a learner to name the piece they think is in danger, then point to the square that changes that danger. That small act gives a coach, a parent, or the learner a way to discuss a decision instead of praising a result alone. Now keep that same position in mind. The next screen is the test.

scenes.label: The handoff
scenes.narration: When the player moves from exploration into computer play, a reset would break the thread of the lesson. The second public capture shows the transfer into play. The important design choice is continuity: the position being studied must still be the position that gets answered. Otherwise the tutorial becomes a separate room with no doorway into the game. I have seen learning tools do that. They explain one thing beautifully, then send the learner somewhere else and ask them to reconstruct the context alone. I wanted Dark Castle Chess to carry more of that burden. Compare these two screens. Look at the board state and at the action that starts the response. If the state has carried through, the player can test the reason they gave a moment ago. If it has not, even a polished coaching message arrives too late to connect to the choice.

scenes.label: The response
scenes.narration: Now the computer answers. The third public capture shows the response with coaching and notation. Here is where the original reason meets a consequence. Maybe the threat was real. Maybe another piece became exposed. Maybe the move was legal and still missed the stronger idea. The screen offers material for reflection, but I want to keep the claim precise: these captures show product behavior, not measured improvement in chess skill. A useful next question is, what changed after the reply? Point to the board before reaching for the label on the move. Then read the coaching and notation as an explanation you can test against what is visible. That order matters. A confident label can stop a learner from looking. A visible consequence invites them to look again. This is the first payoff: the move is no longer an isolated event.

scenes.label: A small learning loop
scenes.narration: The loop is simple enough to remember: inspect, choose, meet the response, explain what changed. I designed the sequence around that rhythm because learning should not depend on the player remembering a detached lesson five minutes later. The position is the shared object. The decision is the hinge. The reply gives the learner another chance to inspect their reasoning. Notice that I am not promising the game will always know the best explanation for every player. A computer can calculate positions; teaching still asks for judgment about what a person needs to understand. That is why I want the product to make its evidence available to a human conversation. A parent can ask what the player expected. A coach can ask what surprised them. The learner can compare their first explanation with the board after the reply.

scenes.label: What a completion screen misses
scenes.narration: Imagine a lesson that ends with a green check and a score. The player may feel good, and sometimes that is enough to keep going. But the check does not tell us whether the next unfamiliar position will make sense. When I look at the Dark Castle sequence, I see a better unit of work: one decision with a before and an after. It is small, but it is inspectable. We can ask where the player's attention went, what the reply revealed, and whether the explanation would still make sense if the pieces changed. This is also a product lesson beyond chess. If you build a learning experience, keep the evidence of the user's decision close to the feedback. Give people a path back to the moment where they chose. The more context they must reconstruct, the more work the product has quietly handed back to them.

scenes.label: The boundary
scenes.narration: There is a boundary I want to say out loud. These public gameplay screens show an Explore position, transfer into play, and a computer response with coaching. They do not show a controlled study, long term retention, or a measured gain in skill. I will not ask the images to carry a claim they cannot carry. What they can show is the architecture of a lesson: the same decision remains visible while the player meets its consequence. That is a design hypothesis worth testing with real learners. I would watch whether they can explain the move before and after the reply, and whether the second explanation grows more precise. I would also watch where they get lost. A beautiful board does not remove confusion by itself. The questions around the board decide whether the experience teaches.

scenes.label: Payoff and invitation
scenes.narration: Return to the first position. Two players made the same move. The product cannot declare that they learned the same thing. It can make the reasoning easier to see and easier to revisit. That is why I rebuilt this lesson around the decision. The board, the handoff, and the reply form one thread a learner can follow. Completion tells us a move happened. A visible decision and its consequence give us something to discuss, challenge, and remember. If you teach chess, build learning tools, or learn by playing, try this with one position: ask for the reason before the move, then ask what changed after the answer. Tell me where that conversation gets clearer or breaks down. Subscribe to AmaduTown for more behind the build lessons about products that make human judgment visible.

packets.title: The AI Cost That Never Appears on the Invoice
packets.rejection_reason: Candidate A has the clearer integrated receipt-pull concept

scenes.label: The missing line
scenes.narration: The invoice says twenty dollars a month. Then someone spends an hour checking the answer, another hour fixing a handoff, and a manager has to decide who owns the mistake. Those hours never appear on the software bill. I built the AI Audit Calculator because a price tag is a poor map of the work surrounding a tool. In this video I will walk through the real calculator screen and a practical way to count the work that moves, grows, or disappears when AI enters a workflow. Keep one question with you: who owns the cleanup when the answer is wrong? By the end, you will have a way to ask that question before signing up for another tool. Start with a simple task your team already does. Name the person who receives the output. Now follow the work after the output arrives.

scenes.label: A workflow, not a license
scenes.narration: Most buying conversations start with seats and subscription tiers. That is easy to compare. The hard part is tracing one job from request to accepted result. Suppose a team uses AI to draft a response. Someone supplies context. Someone reviews accuracy and tone. Someone corrects missing facts. Someone sends the final version and answers for its consequences. If the tool removes twenty minutes of drafting but adds thirty minutes of review, the monthly fee tells only a small part of the story. Before running a calculator, I would draw that path on paper. Mark the hands that touch the work and the points where it waits. Do it with one real workflow, not a vague promise that AI will make everyone faster. The first pattern interrupt is a blank line on the invoice. Write the review time there. The economics look different immediately.

scenes.label: The calculator screen
scenes.narration: This is the AI Audit Calculator screen. The visible interface organizes the assessment into scored dimensions and action guidance. It gives an operator a place to inspect how an AI tool fits into the work, instead of letting a subscription charge stand in for value. I want to be careful about what this image proves. It proves that the product presents an audit view and guidance. It does not prove a customer's return on investment, and it does not prove that a recommendation has been implemented. Use the screen as a prompt for a better conversation. What task is this tool serving? Who reviews its output? What gets escalated? What evidence remains when the team has to explain a decision? Those questions turn a software list into an operating picture. Pause on the guidance area and ask which action you could actually take this week.

scenes.label: The four costs
scenes.narration: I look for four kinds of cost around an AI workflow. First is the visible bill: seats, usage, and integrations. Second is review: the human time required to decide whether an answer is safe and useful. Third is repair: rework after the output misses context, breaks a process, or reaches the wrong person. Fourth is coordination: the time spent clarifying ownership, exceptions, and handoffs. Those categories are a practical checklist, not a universal accounting standard. A small team may feel the coordination cost most sharply because the same person often wears every hat. A larger team may hide it across departments. Either way, the question is concrete: when the tool answers, what work begins? Write that work down before claiming savings. The useful comparison is the same task with and without the tool, measured to an accepted result.

scenes.label: A one-task audit
scenes.narration: Pick one recurring task and give it a name. Count how often it happens in a month. Record the minutes spent preparing input, reviewing output, correcting errors, and handing the result to the next person. Then record those same steps in the existing process. Keep the quality bar equal. If one path creates a fast draft that nobody can use, it has not finished the job. If an experienced worker quietly fixes every answer, include that work. The calculator's assessment can help frame the decision, but the inputs must come from observation. This is where I would ask two people to walk the same job: the person buying the tool and the person cleaning up after it. Their accounts may differ. That difference is evidence worth investigating, not a nuisance to average away. The hidden cost often sits between those two views.

scenes.label: Who owns the exception?
scenes.narration: Now change one condition. The source information is incomplete, or a request falls outside the normal rule. Where does the AI output go? If the system has no named owner for exceptions, the cleanup becomes everybody's problem and nobody's measured work. In an audit, I want to see a decision path: who can accept, revise, refuse, or escalate the result? How do they know which choice is theirs? Where is the record when someone asks what happened? This is a governance question with a cost attached. It affects trust, time, and sometimes the dignity of a customer or colleague who has to repeat the same facts. A useful AI system should make the next responsible action clearer. If it makes the exception harder to find, the low monthly price is misleading.

scenes.label: From score to action
scenes.narration: A score can focus attention, but it cannot manage the change for you. Look at the calculator's action guidance as a starting point for a small test. Choose one workflow. Assign an owner. Decide what an acceptable output looks like. Track preparation, review, repair, and escalation for a bounded period. Then compare that evidence with the current process. If the tool helps, keep the part that helps and write down the conditions under which it works. If the tool adds work, say so. That answer can save the team more than a flattering dashboard. I built the calculator to make these conversations less vague. The people doing the work already know where the friction lives. The audit should give them a place to name it and a way to test whether a proposed fix actually reduces it.

scenes.label: The decision
scenes.narration: Return to the invoice. The subscription price still matters. It is simply one line in a larger operating bill. The team also pays with review time, repair, coordination, and the attention of people asked to catch what the system misses. The AI Audit Calculator makes those dimensions visible enough to discuss; the real workflow supplies the measurements. A tool earns its place when the team can trace the work it removed, the decision it improved, and the evidence it left behind. Take one AI tool you already use and map a single task all the way to an accepted result. Ask who owns the cleanup, then count the time. Tell me what line you found that your invoice missed. Use the AI Audit Calculator to begin that audit, and subscribe to AmaduTown for more practical ways to govern AI investments.
